claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and lack of amino acid pool changes.

claims.claim: Gap1 has been reported to be a 'transceptor' capable of activating protein kinase A (PKA) in a cAMP-independent manner.
claims.source: Gap1 has been reported to be a 'transceptor', that is a protein combining the properties of transporters and receptors, capable of activating protein kinase A (PKA) in a cAMP-independent manner (Donaton et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Conformational changes of Gap1, triggered by binding and/or transport of amino acids, would stimulate a PKA-targeting signaling pathway.
claims.source: According to this model, conformational changes of Gap1, triggered by binding and/or transport of amino acids, would stimulate a PKA-targeting signaling pathway (Schothorst et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature describing the transceptor model.

claims.claim: Gap1 interacts with Gtr2.
claims.source: This hypothesis is potentially supported by a previous report that Gap1 interacts with Gtr2 (Gao and Kaiser, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The high-affinity proline permease Put4 catalyzes β-alanine transport.
claims.source: Confirming a previous prediction (Gournas et al., 2015), we found the high-affinity proline permease Put4 also to catalyze β-ala transport.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous prediction and experimental data.

claims.claim: In proline-free media, the gap1∆ mutant displays residual uptake of β-alanine, which is abolished in the gap1∆ put4∆ mutant.
claims.source: Under these conditions, the gap1∆ mutant displayed residual uptake of β-ala (2 mM), and this uptake was abolished in the gap1∆ put4∆ mutant (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Put4-dependent β-alanine uptake is associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
claims.source: Importantly, this Put4-dependent β-ala uptake was associated with a Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: HcGap1 shares approximately 30% sequence identity with Gap1 and Put4.
claims.source: HcGap1 shares ~ 30% sequence identity with Gap1 and Put4.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claims.claim: In proline-grown gap1∆ cells, HcGap1 restores high β-alanine uptake activity.
claims.source: In proline-grown gap1∆ cells, HcGap1 restored high β-ala uptake activity, roughly similar to that conferred by Put4 to urea-grown cells (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: HcGap1-mediated uptake of β-alanine is associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
claims.source: Remarkably, this uptake of β-ala was also associated with Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Transport of β-alanine via endogenous Gap1 and/or Put4 or via the heterologous HcGap1 permease elicits TORC1 activation.
claims.source: In conclusion, transport of β-ala via endogenous Gap1 and/or Put4 or via the heterologous HcGap1 permease elicits TORC1 activation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation with multiple permeases.

claims.claim: Arginine uptake by proline-grown cells is mediated by Gap1 and the arginine-specific permease Can1.
claims.source: Uptake of arginine (Arg) by proline-grown cells is known to be mediated by Gap1 and the arginine-specific permease Can1 (Wiame et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: High arginine uptake activity is measured in wild type and in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but none in the gap1∆ can1∆ double mutant.
claims.source: Consistently, we measured high Arg uptake activity in the wild type and in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but none in the gap1∆ can1∆ double mutant (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Can1, in contrast to Gap1, does not stimulate PKA upon substrate transport.
claims.source: According to a previous report, Can1, in contrast to Gap1, does not stimulate PKA upon substrate transport (Donaton et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Arginine uptake into wild-type cells induces Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation.
claims.source: Arg uptake into wild-type cells was indeed found to induce Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Arginine-elicited TORC1 activation is impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant.
claims.source: This response was impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant, an effect not due to decreased Arg uptake (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Arginine-elicited TORC1 activation results in Sch9 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Arg-elicited TORC1 activation also resulted in Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 3C), as previously reported (Stracka et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon arginine addition is detected in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but not in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain.
claims.source: Increased phosphorylation of Npr1 upon Arg addition was also detected in gap1∆ and can1∆ single mutants, but not in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both Gap1 and Can1 can promote arginine-induced TORC1 activation.
claims.source: This shows that both permeases can promote Arg-induced TORC1 activation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation in single mutants.

claims.claim: HcGap1 expressed in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain restores high arginine uptake.
claims.source: We next expressed HcGap1 in the gap1∆ can1∆ strain and found it to restore high Arg uptake (Figure 3D) associated with Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Arginine catabolism requires arginase (Car1).
claims.source: Arginine catabolism requires arginase (Car1) (Wiame et al., 1985), so a car1 mutant fails to grow on Arg as sole N source (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Arginine addition to the car1 mutant results in Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation.
claims.source: Arg addition to the car1 mutant also resulted in Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: TORC1 is activated upon arginine uptake via the endogenous Gap1 and/or Can1 or the heterologous HcGap1 permease.
claims.source: In conclusion, TORC1 is activated upon Arg uptake via the endogenous Gap1 and/or Can1 or the heterologous HcGap1 permease.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation with multiple permeases.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation by arginine involves the Rag GTPases and occurs even if arginine is not catabolized.
claims.source: This activation of TORC1 involves the Rag GTPases and occurs even if Arg is not catabolized.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and activation in car1 mutant.

claims.claim: Gap1, Put4, Can1, and HcGap1 behave as H+-symporters.
claims.source: Hence, as expected, all four permeases analyzed in our study, including HcGap1, behave as H+-symporters.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing FCCP and glucose starvation effects on uptake.

claims.claim: Incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore causes a strong reduction of β-alanine uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1.
claims.source: In support of this view, incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore caused a strong reduction of β-ala uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1 and of Arg uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1 (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: Incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore causes a strong reduction of arginine uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1.
claims.source: In support of this view, incubation of cells with the FCCP protonophore caused a strong reduction of β-ala uptake via Gap1, Put4, or HcGap1 and of Arg uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1 (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: Each permease (Gap1, Put4, Can1, HcGap1) is rapidly inhibited when cells are shifted to glucose-free medium.
claims.source: Furthermore, each permease was rapidly inhibited when the cells were shifted to glucose-free medium (Figure 4A and B), a condition known to cause rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and thus collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient (Kane, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B and citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Glucose starvation causes rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient.
claims.source: Furthermore, each permease was rapidly inhibited when the cells were shifted to glucose-free medium (Figure 4A and B), a condition known to cause rapid inhibition of the Pma1 H+-ATPase and thus collapse of the plasma membrane H+ gradient (Kane, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Uptake of cytosine via the Fcy2 permease is coupled to H+ influx.
claims.source: We chose cytosine, whose uptake via the Fcy2 permease is known to be coupled to H+ influx (Pinson et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Addition of cytosine causes rapid activation of TORC1, as judged by increased Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation.
claims.source: Interestingly, addition of cytosine did cause rapid activation of TORC1, as judged by increased Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: Cytosine-elicited TORC1 activation is largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant.
claims.source: Furthermore, this cytosine-elicited TORC1 activation was largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Cytosine can be used as sole N source.
claims.source: Cytosine can be used as sole N source, and thus as a source of amino acids.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of cytosine metabolism.

claims.claim: In an fcy1 mutant lacking cytosine deaminase, Npr1 is still phosphorylated upon cytosine addition.
claims.source: Yet in an fcy1 mutant lacking cytosine deaminase and thus unable to use cytosine as an N source, Npr1 was still phosphorylated upon cytosine addition, unless Rap was also present (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: H+-coupled uptake of cytosine stimulates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner, even when the nucleobase is not assimilated into amino acids.
claims.source: H+-coupled uptake of cytosine thus stimulates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner, even when the nucleobase is not assimilated into amino acids.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation in fcy1 mutant.

claims.claim: Hexoses including fructose enter cells via several Hxt transporters that function as facilitators.
claims.source: Hexoses including fructose are known to enter cells via several Hxt transporters that function as facilitators (Wieczorke et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Particular S. cerevisiae strains express an H+-coupled specific fructose transporter called Fsy1.
claims.source: Yet particular S. cerevisiae strains are reported to also express an H+-coupled specific fructose transporter called Fsy1 (Galeote et al., 2010; Rodrigues de Sousa et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Equivalent fructose uptake is measured in Hxt- and Fsy1-expressing cells under the experimental conditions used.
claims.source: Using these growth conditions, we measured equivalent 14C-fructose uptake in Hxt- and Fsy1-expressing cells (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Fructose uptake via Fsy1 is inhibited in the presence of FCCP, but uptake mediated by the Hxt facilitators is not.
claims.source: Furthermore, fructose uptake via Fsy1 was inhibited in the presence of FCCP, but uptake mediated by the Hxt facilitators was not (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: A Rap-sensitive increase of Sch9 phosphorylation is observed upon fructose uptake by Fsy1-expressing cells.
claims.source: We observed a Rap-sensitive increase of Sch9 phosphorylation upon fructose uptake by Fsy1-expressing cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation is not observed in the wild-type incorporating fructose via the Hxt facilitators.
claims.source: Such a TORC1 activation was observed neither in the wild-type incorporating fructose via the Hxt facilitators nor in the hxt null mutant expressing none fructose transporter (Figure 4I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation in response to fructose uptake occurs only when this transport is coupled to H+ influx.
claims.source: TORC1 activation in response to fructose uptake thus occurred only when this transport was coupled to H+ influx.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data comparing Fsy1 and Hxt-mediated uptake.

claims.claim: FCCP causes the cytosolic pH to drop to about 6.1, the pH of the buffered growth medium.
claims.source: Using a strain stably expressing pHluorin, we first observed that the ionophore caused the cytosolic pH to drop to about 6.1, the pH of the buffered growth medium (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Rapid acidification of the cytosol by FCCP coincides with hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
claims.source: Remarkably, this rapid acidification of the cytosol coincided with hyperphosphorylation of Npr1, and this response was inhibited by Rap (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: H+ influx mediated by a protonophore results in TORC1 stimulation.
claims.source: Hence, H+ influx mediated by a protonophore also results in TORC1 stimulation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Npr1 hyperphosphorylation upon FCCP treatment.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation by FCCP does not lead to increased phosphorylation of Sch9.
claims.source: Yet this TORC1 activation, intriguingly, did not lead to increased phosphorylation of Sch9 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: When the cytosol becomes too acidic, an additional control likely impedes phosphorylation of Sch9 by activated TORC1.
claims.source: A likely explanation is that an additional control elicited when the cytosol becomes too acidic (a stressful condition) impedes phosphorylation of Sch9 by activated TORC1.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lack of Sch9 phosphorylation.

claims.claim: When the cytosolic pH drops to values around 6, the action of TORC1 on Sch9 is inhibited, whereas nitrogen control of the Gat1 and Gln3 transcription factors via TORC1 remains unaltered.
claims.source: This is in keeping with a previous report that when the cytosolic pH drops to values around 6 (as occurs under glucose starvation or when expression of the Pma1 H+-ATPase is repressed), the action of TORC1 on Sch9 is inhibited, whereas nitrogen control of the Gat1 and Gln3 transcription factors via TORC1 remains unaltered (Dechant et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation in response to FCCP-mediated H+ influx is largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain.
claims.source: TORC1 activation in response to an FCCP-mediated H+ influx, thus visible on immunoblots for HA-Npr1, was largely impaired in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain (Figure 5D), indicating that it is Rag/Gtr-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The multisubunit SEACIT complex antagonizes TORC1 by acting as a GAP on the Gtr1 GTPase.
claims.source: The multisubunit SEACIT complex antagonizes TORC1 by acting as a GAP on the Gtr1 GTPase, and its function is itself negatively controlled by the multisubunit SEACAT complex (Panchaud et al., 2013a, 2013b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: TORC1 activation by FCCP is largely impaired in the seh1∆ mutant.
claims.source: TORC1 activation was largely impaired in the seh1∆ mutant (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: In the iml1∆ mutant, a high basal phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 is detected.
claims.source: In the iml1∆ mutant, a high basal phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 was detected, as expected, and FCCP did not significantly further increase this phosphorylation, at least during the first minutes after its addition (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The SEACIT/SEACAT upstream regulators of Gtr1 are involved in H+-influx-elicited stimulation of TORC1 activity.
claims.source: These results indicate that the SEACIT/SEACAT upstream regulators of Gtr1 are involved in H+-influx-elicited stimulation of TORC1 activity.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing effects in seh1∆ and iml1∆ mutants.

claims.claim: The amount of HA-Npr1 is much reduced in seh1∆ mutant cells.
claims.source: We also found the amount of HA-Npr1 to be much reduced in seh1∆ mutant cells, and a similar effect though less pronounced was observed in the gtr1∆ gtr2∆ strain (Figures 1G, 4E and 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The abundance of HA-Npr1 is influenced by the activation state of TORC1.
claims.source: This suggests that the abundance of HA-Npr1 is influenced by the activation state of TORC1.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced HA-Npr1 in mutants with altered TORC1 activity.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 increases after prolonged incubation with FCCP in gtr1∆ gtr2∆, seh1∆, and iml1∆ mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, phosphorylation of HA-Npr1 in the above-analyzed mutants was found to increase after prolonged incubation with FCCP (Figure 5D, E and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5D, E, and F.

claims.claim: FCCP stimulates another mechanism of TORC1 activation that does not depend on the Rag/Gtr GTPases.
claims.source: It thus seems that FCCP stimulates another mechanism of TORC1 activation that does not depend on the Rag/Gtr GTPases.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of delayed TORC1 activation in Gtr mutants.

claims.claim: The vacuole-associated Pib2 protein containing a FYVE domain acts in parallel with Gtr1 to promote TORC1 activation.
claims.source: It has in fact been reported that the vacuole-associated Pib2 protein containing a FYVE domain acts in parallel with Gtr1 to promote TORC1 activation (Kim and Cunningham, 2015; Varlakhanova et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: In an in vitro TORC1 kinase assay using isolated vacuoles, the addition of glutamine stimulates TORC1 activity in a manner dependent on Pib2 but not Gtr1.
claims.source: Furthermore, in an in vitro TORC1 kinase assay using isolated vacuoles, the addition of glutamine was found to stimulate TORC1 activity in a manner dependent on Pib2 but not Gtr1 (Tanigawa and Maeda, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: HA-Npr1 is normally hyperphosphorylated after FCCP addition to pib2∆ mutant cells.
claims.source: We thus also analyzed the role of Pib2 and found that HA-Npr1 is normally hyperphosphorylated after FCCP addition to pib2∆ mutant cells (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: H+ influx mediated by a protonophore elicits a cellular response resulting in Rag/Gtr-dependent, Pib2-independent, TORC1 activation.
claims.source: In conclusion, the above experiments indicate that H+ influx mediated even by a protonophore elicits a cellular response resulting in Rag/Gtr-dependent, Pib2-independent, TORC1 activation.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing Gtr-dependence and Pib2-independence.

claims.claim: Addition of amino acids, cytosine, or NH4+ to growing cells does not detectably change their cytosolic pH.
claims.source: We observed that addition of amino acids, cytosine, or NH4+ to growing cells does not detectably change their cytosolic pH (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claims.claim: The cytosol has high buffering capacity.
claims.source: This was expected, given the high buffering capacity of the cytosol and the compensating H+ efflux activity of the Pma1 H+-ATPase, which is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present (Eraso and Gancedo, 1987; Ullah et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on cytosolic buffering.

claims.claim: The Pma1 H+-ATPase is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present.
claims.source: This was expected, given the high buffering capacity of the cytosol and the compensating H+ efflux activity of the Pma1 H+-ATPase, which is stimulated under acidic conditions as long as glucose is present (Eraso and Gancedo, 1987; Ullah et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The vacuolar V-ATPase catalyzes ATP-dependent uptake of H+ into the vacuole to acidify the organelle, compensate for constant H+ efflux, and control cytosolic pH.
claims.source: An H+ increase can in principle be caused by inhibition of the vacuolar V-ATPase, as this enzymatic complex catalyzes ATP-dependent uptake of H+ into the vacuole in order to acidify the organelle, to compensate for the constant H+ efflux mediated by H+-coupled vacuolar transporters, and to control the cytosolic pH (Kane, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on V-ATPase function.

claims.claim: Addition of concanamycin A (CMA) to proline-grown cells does not significantly change the cytosolic pH.
claims.source: Addition of CMA to proline-grown cells did not significantly change the cytosolic pH of the cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Pma1-dependent efflux and the buffering capacity of the cytosol prevent the expected increase in cytosolic H+ upon CMA treatment.
claims.source: This suggests that Pma1-dependent efflux and the buffering capacity of the cytosol prevented the expected increase in cytosolic H+.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of pH change despite V-ATPase inhibition.

claims.claim: BAF addition causes a slight but significant drop in the cytosolic pH.
claims.source: BAF addition did cause a slight but significant drop in the cytosolic pH, suggesting that this treatment caused stronger inhibition of the V-ATPase (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Both CMA and BAF treatment result in stimulation of TORC1 activity, as judged by Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1.
claims.source: Remarkably, both CMA and BAF treatment resulted in stimulation of TORC1 activity, as judged by Rap-sensitive hyperphosphorylation of Npr1 (Figure 6B and Figure 6F, respectively) and by a transient increase in Sch9 phosphorylation (Figure 6C and Figure 6G, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B, 6C, 6F, and 6G.

claims.claim: No increase in Npr1 phosphorylation is detected in either CMA- or BAF-treated gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells.
claims.source: No increase in Npr1 phosphorylation was detected in either CMA- or BAF-treated gtr1∆ gtr2∆ mutant cells (Figure 6D and H, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6D and 6H.

claims.claim: Inhibition of the V-ATPase is associated with efficient Rag/Gtr-dependent stimulation of TORC1 activity.
claims.source: We conclude that inhibition of the V-ATPase is associated with efficient Rag/Gtr-dependent stimulation of TORC1 activity, even when this inhibition is not sufficient to cause a detectable lowering of the cytosolic pH.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing TORC1 activation by V-ATPase inhibitors.

claims.claim: Several plant H+-ATPases are active when expressed in yeast strains where PMA1 and PMA2 are deleted or repressed.
claims.source: According to previous reports, several plant H+-ATPases are active when expressed in yeast strains where the essential PMA1 gene and its non-essential paralog PMA2 (expressed to a much lower level) are deleted or repressed (Morsomme et al., 2000; Palmgren and Christensen, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Wild-type forms of plant H+-ATPases typically compensate only partially for the lack of Pma1.
claims.source: The wild-type forms of these plant H+-ATPases typically compensate only partially for the lack of Pma1.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous literature on plant H+-ATPase expression in yeast.

claims.claim: It is possible to isolate mutant derivatives of plant H+-ATPases sustaining faster growth, particularly on low-pH media.
claims.source: It is possible, however, to isolate mutant derivatives sustaining faster growth, particularly on low-pH media where cells need high H+-ATPase activity to maintain a neutral cytosolic pH (Morsomme et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The H+-ATPase Pma4 of tobacco restores limited growth to a pma1∆ pma2∆ double-null mutant.
claims.source: For instance, the H+-ATPase Pma4 of tobacco (Nicotiana plumbaginifolia) restores limited growth to a pma1∆ pma2∆ double-null mutant.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous literature on plant H+-ATPase expression in yeast.

claims.claim: A truncated Pma4 protein called Pma4882ochre, lacking the last 71 C-terminal amino acids, is able to support faster growth of yeast pma1∆ pma2∆ cells.
claims.source: A truncated Pma4 protein called Pma4882ochre, lacking the last 71 C-terminal amino acids as a result of an ochre nonsense mutation in codon 882 of the PMA4 gene, is able to support faster growth of yeast pma1∆ pma2∆ cells (Luo et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Cells expressing PMA4822ochre grow more slowly than cells expressing PMA1.
claims.source: We found cells expressing PMA4822ochre to grow more slowly (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The mutant plant H+-ATPase does not fully compensate for the lack of Pma1.
claims.source: This shows that the mutant plant H+-ATPase does not fully compensate for the lack of Pma1.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the growth data.

claims.claim: The cytosolic pH of PMA4822ochre-expressing cells is slightly lower than that of PMA1-expressing cells.
claims.source: Accordingly, compared to the cytosolic pH of PMA1-expressing cells, that of PMA4822ochre-expressing cells was slightly lower (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: H+-coupled uptake of β-alanine is significantly lower in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells compared to PMA1-expressing cells.
claims.source: H+-coupled uptake of β-ala (1 mM) was also significantly lower in the latter cells (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations (data not shown).

claims.claim: β-alanine uptake is coupled to H+ influx in both PMA1- and PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
claims.source: As expected, and whichever gene was expressed, [14C]-β-ala uptake was inhibited after a brief treatment of the cells with FCCP. This shows that in both cases, β-ala uptake is coupled to H+ influx (Figure 7D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claims.claim: Upon transfer to glucose-free medium, uptake of β-alanine into PMA1-expressing cells is strongly reduced.
claims.source: Upon transfer of the cells to a glucose-free medium, uptake of β-ala into PMA1-expressing cells was also strongly reduced (Figure 7D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claims.claim: The reduction in β-alanine uptake upon glucose starvation is much less pronounced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells.
claims.source: This reduction was much less pronounced in PMA4822ochre-expressing cells (Figure 7D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7D and 7F.

claims.claim: Inactivation of H+-ATPases upon glucose starvation requires a C-terminal auto-inhibitory region which the truncated protein Pma4822ochre lacks.
claims.source: This result can be readily explained by the fact that inactivation of H+-ATPases upon glucose starvation, a regulation conserved between yeast and plant H+-ATPases, requires a C-terminal auto-inhibitory region which the truncated protein Pma4822ochre lacks (Morsomme et al., 2000; Portillo, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on H+-ATPase regulation.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of Npr1 increases moderately upon addition of β-alanine at low concentration to PMA1-expressing cells.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of Npr1 was found to increase moderately upon addition of β-ala at low concentration (0.1 mM) to PMA1-expressing cells, but this variation was significant, as judged by its sensitivity to Rap (Figure 7E).

results.result: β-alanine uptake via Gap1 activates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner without increasing internal amino acid pools. β-alanine is transported by Gap1, cannot serve as a nitrogen source, yet triggers TORC1 activation as evidenced by Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation. This activation is impaired in gap1Δ and gtr1Δ gtr2Δ mutants and does not result from conversion of β-alanine to other amino acids.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C51 provide converging evidence from uptake assays (C38, C48), growth assays (C39), ubiquitination and localization studies (C42-C45), phosphorylation assays (C46-C47), genetic analysis (C48, C50), and amino acid pool measurements (C49). The data consistently demonstrate that β-alanine uptake via Gap1 activates TORC1 through a Rag/Gtr-dependent mechanism independent of amino acid metabolism.

results.result: β-alanine transport via Put4 or the heterologous HcGap1 permease also activates TORC1. Put4 mediates β-alanine uptake in gap1Δ cells, and HcGap1 from H. cylindrosporum restores β-alanine uptake in gap1Δ cells. Both permeases trigger Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation upon β-alanine addition.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 demonstrate through uptake assays (C56, C59) and phosphorylation analysis (C57, C60) that multiple permeases can mediate TORC1 activation by β-alanine. The use of both an endogenous permease (Put4) and a heterologous permease (HcGap1) strengthens the conclusion that the transport process itself, rather than a specific permease, triggers TORC1 activation.

results.result: Arginine uptake via Gap1, Can1, or HcGap1 activates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner even without arginine catabolism. Both Gap1 and Can1 mediate arginine uptake and trigger TORC1 activation. HcGap1 can substitute for endogenous permeases. TORC1 activation occurs in car1 mutants unable to catabolize arginine.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C74 provide comprehensive evidence from uptake assays (C63, C70), phosphorylation analysis (C65, C67, C68, C72), genetic analysis (C66, C71), and use of multiple permeases (C69, C73). The demonstration that TORC1 activation occurs in car1 mutants (C72, C74) is particularly important as it shows the response is independent of arginine metabolism, paralleling the β-alanine results.

results.result: Gap1, Put4, Can1, and HcGap1 function as H+-symporters. All four permeases show FCCP-sensitive uptake and are inhibited by glucose starvation, which collapses the plasma membrane H+ gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 establish the H+-coupled nature of transport through pharmacological (FCCP treatment, C76-C77) and physiological (glucose starvation, C78) approaches. The consistent behavior across all four permeases (C75) and citation to established knowledge about glucose starvation effects (C79) provide strong support.

results.result: H+-coupled cytosine uptake via Fcy2 activates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner even when cytosine is not metabolized. Cytosine addition triggers Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation, this response is impaired in gtr1Δ gtr2Δ mutants, and occurs in fcy1 mutants lacking cytosine deaminase.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 extend the findings to a non-amino acid nutrient. The use of fcy1 mutants (C84) that cannot metabolize cytosine (C83) is a critical control demonstrating that TORC1 activation is independent of nutrient assimilation, similar to the β-alanine and arginine results. The Gtr-dependence (C82) is consistent with previous findings.

results.result: H+-coupled fructose uptake via Fsy1, but not passive uptake via Hxt facilitators, activates TORC1. Fructose uptake via the H+-symporter Fsy1 is FCCP-sensitive and triggers Sch9 phosphorylation, while equivalent uptake via Hxt facilitators does not activate TORC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 provide a critical comparison between H+-coupled and passive transport of the same nutrient. The demonstration that only H+-coupled transport activates TORC1 (C92), with equivalent uptake rates (C88) and FCCP sensitivity distinguishing the two modes (C89), strongly supports the hypothesis that H+ influx is the activating signal. This is a key experiment distinguishing nutrient uptake from H+ influx.

results.result: FCCP-mediated H+ influx activates TORC1 as measured by Npr1 phosphorylation but not Sch9 phosphorylation. FCCP causes cytosolic acidification to pH 6.1 and triggers Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation. However, Sch9 phosphorylation is not increased, likely due to an additional control mechanism activated by excessive cytosolic acidification.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 demonstrate TORC1 activation by H+ influx independent of nutrient transport. The dissociation between Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation (C96) is explained by previous literature (C98) showing differential regulation under acidic stress. This supports the model while revealing complexity in TORC1 signaling under extreme pH conditions.

results.result: FCCP-induced TORC1 activation requires the Rag/Gtr GTPases and their SEACIT/SEACAT regulators. TORC1 activation by FCCP is impaired in gtr1Δ gtr2Δ, seh1Δ, and iml1Δ mutants. Prolonged FCCP treatment may activate a Rag/Gtr-independent mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C107 establish the genetic requirements for H+-induced TORC1 activation. The analysis of multiple mutants (C99, C101, C102) in the Rag/Gtr pathway provides strong evidence for pathway involvement. The observation of delayed activation in mutants (C106-C107) suggests pathway complexity but does not undermine the primary conclusion about Rag/Gtr dependence.

results.result: FCCP-induced TORC1 activation does not require Pib2. HA-Npr1 is normally hyperphosphorylated after FCCP addition to pib2Δ mutant cells, indicating that H+ influx-mediated TORC1 activation is Pib2-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 distinguish the H+ influx pathway from the Pib2-dependent pathway. The normal response in pib2Δ mutants (C110) contrasts with the requirement for Pib2 in glutamine-stimulated TORC1 activation in vitro (C109), supporting the existence of parallel pathways.

results.result: V-ATPase inhibition activates TORC1 in a Rag/Gtr-dependent manner. Treatment with concanamycin A or bafilomycin A stimulates TORC1 activity as measured by Npr1 and Sch9 phosphorylation. This activation is impaired in gtr1Δ gtr2Δ mutants and occurs even without detectable cytosolic pH changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C121 demonstrate that increasing cytosolic H+ by blocking its removal (via V-ATPase inhibition) also activates TORC1. The use of two different inhibitors (C119) and the Gtr-dependence (C120) strengthen the conclusion. The observation that TORC1 activation occurs without detectable pH changes (C116, C121) suggests high sensitivity to H+ or local pH changes.

results.result: Cells expressing the plant H+-ATPase Pma4882ochre instead of Pma1 show reduced growth, slightly lower cytosolic pH, and reduced β-alanine uptake. The plant H+-ATPase partially compensates for Pma1 loss and shows differential regulation upon glucose starvation due to lack of the C-terminal auto-inhibitory region.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C134 establish the baseline characteristics of cells expressing the plant H+-ATPase. The growth data (C127), pH measurements (C129), uptake assays (C130-C133), and mechanistic explanation for glucose starvation differences (C134) provide comprehensive characterization. This is essential groundwork for the subsequent TORC1 activation experiments.

results.result: Pma1 is essential for TORC1 activation in response to H+ influx. β-alanine, FCCP, and BAF fail to activate TORC1 in cells expressing Pma4882ochre instead of Pma1, despite equivalent H+ influx or cytosolic acidification. This demonstrates that Pma1 plays a specific role beyond H+ extrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C144 provide the key evidence for Pma1's role in TORC1 activation. Multiple stimuli (β-alanine, FCCP, BAF) all fail to activate TORC1 in Pma4882ochre-expressing cells (C136, C142, C143) despite causing equivalent pH changes (C140). The comprehensive analysis using both Npr1 and Sch9 as readouts (C135-C139) and multiple activation conditions strengthens the conclusion that Pma1 has a specific signaling function.

results.result: NH4+-induced TORC1 activation occurs independently of both Rag/Gtr GTPases and Pma1. NH4+ triggers Rap-sensitive Npr1 hyperphosphorylation in both wild-type and gtr1Δ gtr2Δ mutants, and in both Pma1- and Pma4882ochre-expressing cells. This suggests Pma1 is specifically required for H+ influx-mediated but not amino acid accumulation-mediated TORC1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C151 provide a critical control demonstrating that TORC1 can be activated in Pma4882ochre-expressing cells (C149-C150), ruling out general TORC1 dysfunction. The Gtr-independence (C146-C147) and dependence on glutamate synthesis (C148) distinguish this pathway from H+ influx-mediated activation. This supports the model that Pma1 is specifically required for sensing H+ influx rather than being generally required for TORC1 function.

results.result: H+ influx coupled to nutrient uptake is the signal triggering Rag/Gtr-dependent TORC1 activation, and Pma1 plays a central role in this mechanism. This activation occurs with multiple nutrients (amino acids, cytosine, fructose), via protonophore-mediated H+ diffusion, and upon V-ATPase inhibition. The response requires Rag/Gtr GTPases but not Pib2, and depends on Pma1.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C158 synthesize the major findings of the study. The convergence of evidence from multiple experimental approaches (different nutrients, pharmacological manipulations, genetic analysis) strongly supports the central conclusion. Each component has been individually validated in previous result groups, and together they form a coherent model.

results.result: The authors propose that H+ influx via derepressed H+-symporters provides a general signal for rapid TORC1 reactivation upon relief from starvation, while sustained activation requires nutrient assimilation. During starvation, cells reduce TORC1 activity and upregulate H+-symporters, positioning them to sense nutrient availability through H+ influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C169 present a speculative model integrating the findings with known starvation responses. While the model is logical and consistent with the data (C159-C163 cite established knowledge, C167 cites supporting literature), the specific predictions about transient versus sustained activation (C164-C168) are not directly tested in this study. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: The authors propose that H+ influx might also activate PKA, offering an alternative to the transceptor model. FCCP addition to N-starved cells stimulates trehalase activity, consistent with PKA activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C173 present an alternative model for PKA activation. While the trehalase activation by FCCP (C173) is consistent with the model, this is limited evidence. The transceptor model (C171) is well-established in the literature, and the proposed alternative (C172) is speculative. Additional experiments directly measuring PKA activity and testing the model in transceptor mutants would be needed.

results.result: The authors propose a two-phase model for glutamine-induced TORC1 activation: rapid Gtr1-dependent activation via H+ influx during uptake, followed by sustained Pib2-dependent activation via intracellular glutamine accumulation. Sustained activation requires Gtr2 as well as Gtr1.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C180 integrate previous literature (C174-C177) with the current findings to propose a model. The model is logical and consistent with available data, but the specific proposal about H+ influx mediating the transient phase (C178) is not directly tested. The observation about Gtr2 requirement (C180) adds complexity but is based on the authors' own observations conflicting with one cited study.

results.result: Sch9 is activated by H+ influx but inhibited by excessive cytosolic acidification. Sch9 contributes to pH homeostasis by controlling V-ATPase activity. Under acidic stress, a mechanism prevents Sch9 phosphorylation by activated TORC1 while Npr1 phosphorylation continues.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C188 explain the differential regulation of Sch9 versus Npr1 observed in FCCP experiments. The integration with recent literature on Sch9's role in pH homeostasis (C182) and previous reports of differential regulation under stress (C188) provides strong support. The model is consistent with the observation that FCCP activates TORC1 (Npr1 phosphorylation) without increasing Sch9 phosphorylation.

results.result: The authors discuss two models for Pma1's role: indirect effects due to incomplete compensation by Pma4882ochre, or direct signaling from Pma1 to TORC1. They favor the signaling model, proposing that Pma1 activity changes in response to H+ influx might be transmitted to TORC1 regulators. Pma1's role as the main ATP consumer positions it to sense cellular energy status.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C197 present two alternative models and arguments for each. The indirect model (C189-C191) is acknowledged but the authors favor the signaling model (C192-C197). However, the signaling model is largely speculative (C195, C197) despite being supported by analogy to Na+/K+-ATPase (discussed in C203-C204). The data do not definitively distinguish between these models, and the authors acknowledge this uncertainty.

results.result: Additional observations support a role for Pma1 in TORC1 regulation: TORC1 is inhibited when Pma1 synthesis is reduced, TORC1 is inhibited during glucose starvation when Pma1 is auto-inhibited, and TORC1 is required for full Pma1 activity, suggesting crosstalk.
results.evaluation: Claims C198-C202 cite multiple lines of evidence from the literature supporting a connection between Pma1 and TORC1. While these observations are correlative rather than mechanistic, they are consistent with the proposed model and strengthen the case for Pma1's involvement in TORC1 regulation. The bidirectional relationship (C202) is particularly interesting.

results.result: The authors tested whether Pma1 might signal to TORC1 via a mechanism analogous to Na+/K+-ATPase signaling to Src. They introduced substitutions in the conserved region of Pma1 corresponding to the Src-binding region of Na+/K+-ATPase, but these variants behaved normally in TORC1 activation assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C206 describe a rational experimental test of the signaling model based on analogy to Na+/K+-ATPase (C203-C204). The negative result (C206) does not disprove the signaling model but suggests the mechanism differs from the Na+/K+-ATPase-Src interaction. This is appropriate follow-up work even though it did not yield positive results.
